items.value: The explosion took place at 4:58:42 PM — the spot is 5400 m away, each drone flight takes 180 s and the sound took 18 s to reach the camp
items.reasoning: The second drone leaves the camp at the instant the first picture arrives (5:02 PM) and its own picture arrives when it reaches the spot (5:05 PM), so a one-way drone flight takes 3 minutes = 180 s. At 30 m/s the distance is 30 x 180 = 5400 m. The first drone also flew for 180 s and started only when the sound reached the camp, so the sound arrived at 5:02:00 - 180 s = 4:59:00 PM. Sound covered 5400 m at 300 m/s in 18 s, so the explosion was 18 s earlier still, at 4:58:42 PM. Option A (4:59:00 PM) is the moment the first drone started, not the moment of the explosion — it is the trap for anyone who forgets the sound lag.

items.value: The unit digit of 6^129 x 7^307 is 8
items.reasoning: Every positive power of 6 ends in 6, so 6^129 ends in 6. The unit digits of powers of 7 cycle with period 4 as 7, 9, 3, 1; since 307 = 4 x 76 + 3, the third member of the cycle applies and 7^307 ends in 3. The product therefore ends in the unit digit of 6 x 3 = 18, which is 8.

items.value: Saving rises by 30% (from 10 to 13 on a salary base of 100)
items.reasoning: Take the salary as 100. Saving is 10% = 10, so expenditure is 90. After the rise the salary is 112 and the expenditure is 90 x 1.10 = 99, so the new saving is 112 - 99 = 13. The increase is 3 on a base of 10, that is 30%. The decrease options are the trap for treating the 10% expenditure rise as if it were applied to the whole salary.

items.value: Q is the sister of R, and R is S's husband — so Q is a sister of the husband of S (her sister-in-law)
items.reasoning: P has exactly one son and one daughter, and Q and R are P's children, so one of Q and R is the son and the other the daughter. S is the mother of T, so S is female, and S is R's spouse, so R is male — R is P's son and Q is P's daughter. Q is therefore R's sister, and since S is married to R, Q is a sister of S's husband. Option A confuses a sister-in-law with a sister; B and C invert the generations, since S is Q's brother's wife and neither Q's mother nor Q's daughter.

The powers of 2 around the three-digit range are 2^6 = 64 (two digits), 2^7 = 128, 2^8 = 256, 2^9 = 512 and 2^10 = 1024 (four digits). Only 128, 256 and 512 lie between 100 and 999, so the count is 3. Negative integral powers of 2 are fractions and cannot be three-digit numbers, so they add nothing.

items.value: Inferences 1 and 3 follow; inference 2 does not, because the passage attributes an effective ban to available alternatives and affordable cost, not to public will or conviction
items.reasoning: Inference 1 restates the passage's opening claim that the key source of the battle for clean skies is the fuel we burn, from chulhas to thermal power plants, so the energy source is indeed the key. Inference 3 is supported by the sentence that the Supreme Court agreed fiscal measures were needed to keep clean fuel cheaper than dirty fuel — that is judicial approval of a fiscal intervention to price cleaner fuel favourably. Inference 2 fails: the stated lesson from the CNG transition is that people need alternatives, and that those alternatives must be feasible in cost; the passage never mentions strength of will or public conviction about the greater good.

items.value: Only statement 2 is correct — CNG supply had to be assured when diesel buses were stopped
items.reasoning: Statement 1 misreports the passage: the agreement was that thermal power plants would clean up OR shut down, not that they were required to shut down summarily. Statement 3 attributes the coal ban to the wrong authority: the passage says the Supreme Court banned pet coke, while it was the Delhi Government that banned coal, a ban later extended to the whole National Capital Region. Statement 2 matches the sentence that when diesel buses were stopped, CNG supply had to be assured; its widening of buses to vehicles is the only slack in it, and it is the sole defensible statement.

items.value: All three follow: P (every blue is yellow), Q (every red is green) and R (every red is yellow)
items.reasoning: The premises give the chain red is contained in blue, blue in green and green in yellow. Chaining blue to green to yellow gives P. Chaining red to blue to green gives Q. Chaining all three links gives R. Universal affirmative statements of this form are transitive, so every one of the three conclusions is valid and the answer is P, Q and R.

items.value: The digit 5 appears 19 times among the two-digit integers 10 to 99
items.reasoning: As a tens digit, 5 occurs in the ten numbers 50 to 59, giving 10 occurrences. As a units digit it occurs in 15, 25, 35, 45, 55, 65, 75, 85 and 95, giving 9 more. The total number of appearances is 10 + 9 = 19; note that 55 contributes twice, once in each place, which is correct when counting appearances of the digit rather than numbers containing it. Answering 18 comes from wrongly excluding one of the two 5s in 55.

items.value: Y finishes 6 minutes earlier — X takes 69 minutes against Y's 63 minutes
items.reasoning: X takes 1/5 h + 2/10 h + 3/4 h = 12 + 12 + 45 = 69 minutes. Y takes 1/4 h + 2/10 h + 3/5 h = 15 + 12 + 36 = 63 minutes. The middle leg is identical for both, so the whole difference comes from the outer legs, and 69 - 63 = 6 minutes. Y gains by spending the slow speed on the short 1 km stretch and the faster speed on the long 3 km stretch.

items.value: Two weighings suffice, and one cannot be enough — split 3, 3 and 1, then split the lighter three as 1, 1 and 1
items.reasoning: Weigh three cubes against three. If they balance, the seventh cube set aside is the light one; if not, the light cube is among the three on the higher pan. In the second weighing put one of those three against another: if they balance the third is light, otherwise the higher one is. A single weighing has only three possible outcomes and so can single out at most three candidates, which is fewer than seven, so one attempt cannot guarantee identification. Two is therefore the minimum that works with certainty.

items.value: The passage's viewpoint is that AI may be beneficial because human agents can be redirected to creative and rewarding work rather than made redundant
items.reasoning: The passage concedes that AI could prove different from earlier waves of customer-service technology, but its own judgement comes in the last two sentences: if AI does prove different, its effects may be salutary, because human agents could be freed up for creative and rewarding tasks such as using feedback to improve products. That is exactly option C. Option D is contradicted, since the passage says the earlier waves also stoked job-loss concerns, and option A states an extreme the passage never approaches. The runner-up is option B, which paraphrases the passage's first two sentences accurately enough; it would win if the question were read as asking for the passage's factual comparison rather than its stance, but B leans toward AI causing redundancy while the passage's point of view pivots away from that to the salutary reading.

items.value: Conclusions 1 and 2 follow; 3 does not, because the passage says the effects may be salutary rather than stressful
items.reasoning: Conclusion 3 is directly contradicted: the passage calls the possible effects salutary and describes agents spending less time with irate customers, so any option containing 3 is out, which removes A and C. Conclusion 2 is supported, since the earlier fears of job losses failed to materialise while the technology did take over certain tasks, and human agents can be redirected to creative and rewarding work. Conclusion 1 restates the opening sentence, that previous waves of customer-service technology stoked concerns of job losses. The runner-up is option B, 2 only; it would win if the word invariably in conclusion 1 is judged too absolute for a passage that names only email and voice menus as examples, and absolute quantifiers are a standard trap in this format — but the passage frames previous waves as a class that did stoke such fears, so 1 reads as a fair restatement.

items.value: Only conclusion 3 follows — a landlord holding to old values is shown as one who looks after his tenants
items.reasoning: Conclusion 3 follows from the closing sentence: Rai Sahib still held to the old values and felt that any landlord who did not look after his tenants was less than human, tying traditional values to concern for tenants. Conclusion 1 fails because the passage explicitly contrasts Rai Sahib with selfish zamindars who would have let the cattle go to hell, so goodness in all landlords is denied rather than implied. Conclusion 2 fails because the cattle grazing there came from the nearby villages, not from one village alone. Conclusion 4 inverts the passage, which places the cool freshness in the morning and the scorching loo wind through the rest of the day.

items.value: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are the incorrect ones; only statement 4, that Rai Sahib valued his tenants and wanted to protect their livelihood, is correct
items.reasoning: The question asks which statements are NOT correct. Statement 1 is wrong because only the common grazing ground is described as not farmed; the passage refers to Rai Sahib's tenants, so his holdings as a whole are clearly farmed. Statement 2 is wrong because he is contrasted with the selfish zamindars and refused a good price. Statement 3 is wrong because the passage settles the point it says cannot be settled: a number of farmers were eager to lease the land and had offered a good price, and the text speaks of his chance to make a little money. Statement 4 is correct, so it is not among the incorrect ones — which leaves 1, 2 and 3.

items.value: 6 km apart, facing North — the path is East 4, South 3, East 2, North 3, ending 6 km due east of the start
items.reasoning: Start at the origin facing East and go 4 km east to (4, 0). A right turn from East faces South, and 3 km gives (4, -3). A left turn from South faces East, and 2 km gives (6, -3). A left turn from East faces North, and 3 km gives (6, 0). The final point is 6 km due east of the start, so the straight-line distance is 6 km, and the last turn left the person facing North. Option B has the right distance but the wrong final facing.

items.value: The sixth term is 47 — the sequence runs 4, 7, 11, 18, 29, 47
items.reasoning: Each term after the first two is the sum of the two immediately before it. Starting from 4 and 7: 4 + 7 = 11, 7 + 11 = 18, 11 + 18 = 29 and 18 + 29 = 47. Counting the two given numbers as the first and second terms makes 47 the sixth. Option A, 29, is the fifth term and is the trap for miscounting the position.

items.value: 23 : 24 — with equal female counts, A totals 23 units against B's 24
items.reasoning: Scale both ratios to a common female count. In A, male to female is 13 : 10; in B it is 7 : 5, which is 14 : 10. If each company has 10 units of female workers, A has 13 male and 10 female, a total of 23, while B has 14 male and 10 female, a total of 24. The ratio of total workers in A to those in B is therefore 23 : 24. Option A reverses the two and is the trap for scaling in the wrong direction.

items.value: Both I and II hold — the numbers must be n and n^2, whose difference n(n-1) is always even and one of which is a perfect square
items.reasoning: For any two positive integers the product of their HCF and LCM equals the product of the numbers themselves. So if that product is the cube of one of them, say a x b = a^3, then b = a^2; the other case a x b = b^3 gives a = b^2. Either way the pair is n and n^2 with n at least 2, since n = 1 would make them equal rather than distinct. Statement II is then immediate, because n^2 is a perfect square. Statement I holds because the difference n^2 - n = n(n - 1) is a product of two consecutive integers, one of which must be even. Checking the pairs (2, 4), (3, 9), (4, 16), (5, 25) and (6, 36) confirms both properties every time.

items.value: The remainder is 7 — divisibility by 11 forces x + y to be 7 or 18, and both leave remainder 7 on division by 11
items.reasoning: For 4x5y790, counting places from the right, the odd places hold 0, 7, 5 and 4 with sum 16, and the even places hold 9, y and x with sum 9 + x + y. Divisibility by 11 requires 16 - (9 + x + y) = 7 - (x + y) to be a multiple of 11, so x + y is congruent to 7 modulo 11. Since x and y are digits, x + y lies between 0 and 18, leaving x + y = 7 or x + y = 18. Both give the same result here: 7 divided by 11 leaves 7, and 18 divided by 11 leaves 7, so the remainder is 7 regardless of which pair of digits is used.
